title: Arsenal Academy host script
timing: Plan 45–60 minutes including discussion and 21 students choosing cards. Short route: take one answer per question, choose one Cinema film, skip Matchday and explore three scouting profiles. Card choosing sets the pace.
use: The big page number and heading match the journal on the classroom display. Setup and optional Matchday are separate stops, not extra journal pages. Read SAY and ASK aloud; CLICK and PAUSE guide you. Keep this script on a second device or print it. Its controls move the script only.

sections.label: Before students arrive
blocks: Open the public Academy. Turn on Full screen; Options → Show room labels can help. Open this script on a separate device or print it. Use the website’s Next page or Contents controls to follow the page cues.

Set out 42 physical cards for 21 students. Know each student’s classroom number 1–21. Keep a paper checklist to confirm two cards per student. Decide who the six captains are before the ceremony; the Vault randomizes stories, not students.

Pre-open A Champion’s Story, the 1:01 Merino trailer, on your presentation device. Check school access, volume and what appears before playback. Return to the Academy after it ends. The prior review covered available captions and 61 frames; it was not a complete audio listen. The owner accepted this trailer’s brief shirtless footage.
North London Forever is the optional 27-second stadium clip you chose. Open it on your presentation device before class if using it. The two classroom cheers work without a recording.
Use a comfortable group voice. Children may join by speaking, gentle clapping, a hand motion or listening. Keep feet and hands in personal space.
Optional Matchday: read the date on the board. Its figures are a manually maintained snapshot, not live scores. For a later presentation, verify the official table before describing them as current.
Pronunciation help: Arsène Wenger ≈ ar-SEN VENG-er; Mikel Merino ≈ MEE-kel meh-REE-noh; Saliba ≈ suh-LEE-buh. Names deserve care; model learning them together.

sections.label: Journal page 1  This is Arsenal
blocks: Stay in the clubhouse for the opening question. The next click opens journal page 1, THIS IS ARSENAL.
All right, important question. Possibly the most important question before lunch.
Who do you think is the best football club in the world?
Invite two or three students. If the room is quiet: “Arsenal? Real Madrid? Barcelona? Bayern Munich? Another team?” Accept their choices warmly.

Excellent answers. And the correct answer, according to your extremely unbiased host, is… Arsenal! You may have detected a tiny amount of favoritism. You can absolutely support a different team. Today you get to discover my favorite.
Who here likes soccer? Who has played? Who has watched a game or cheered for a team? Did anybody watch a World Cup? Who were you rooting for?
Take a few quick answers. Then ask “Favorite player—Messi, Ronaldo, or somebody else?” Welcome players from women’s and men’s football. No knowledge quiz or forced answer.

You already know something about being a teammate or supporter. We notice effort, cheer people on and help someone feel included. Today we are football explorers, scouts and card collectors. I have also promoted myself to stadium announcer. My contract lasts until the bell.
Choose ViewSonic Journal. Confirm the display says 1 / 12 and THIS IS ARSENAL.

This is Arsenal: a football club from London, England, founded in 1886. In England, soccer is usually called football. Same game, different word. Our Academy mission is to discover people and make sure everyone belongs.
Attention cue: you say “Team check!”; class answers “Ready!” and settles. Practise once at a comfortable volume.
Next page → 2 / 12, HOME IS NORTH LONDON.
Journal teacher note: Who here likes soccer? Today you get to discover my favorite team!
sections.teacherNote: Who here likes soccer? Today you get to discover my favorite team!

sections.label: Journal page 2  Home is North London
blocks: Home is North London. This is Emirates Stadium, Arsenal’s home. Imagine a whole stadium cheering for the same team—all those people sharing one very strong opinion about where a ball should go.
What makes a place feel like home? The building? The people? Someone saving you a seat?
Take two answers. Open “What makes a place feel like home?”

A team is stronger when people feel welcome. Think about a big classroom job. If one person does everything, that can be a lot. When we share jobs and listen, we can often get more done and help each other through the tricky parts.
What could a good leader do if someone is left out of the group?

Invite them in. Explain the plan. Listen to their idea. Leadership can be as simple as “Come work with us.” Whether you love football, are brand-new to it or mostly came for the cards, you belong here.
One gentle stadium wave across the room. Students can raise a hand or watch.
Beautiful. Our stadium wave has excellent classroom management.
Journal teacher note: Imagine a whole stadium cheering for the same team!
sections.teacherNote: Imagine a whole stadium cheering for the same team!

sections.label: Journal page 3  The Invincibles
blocks: In 2003–04, Arsenal played 38 Premier League games and lost zero. Zero! I have lost a pencil between taking attendance and putting the attendance sheet down.

Their manager was Arsène Wenger. They became the first team to complete a Premier League season unbeaten, and no other Premier League team has done it since. That is why this team is called the Invincibles.

Historical distinction: Preston North End also went unbeaten in England’s top division in 1888–89, before the Premier League existed. Do not call Arsenal the first unbeaten English team ever. Claim checked against the Premier League archive, 19 November 2026.
They won 26 games and drew 12. A draw means a tied score. How many games is 26 plus 12? And how many defeats are left out of 38?
Open “26 wins + 12 draws. How many defeats?” after the class answers.

Thirty-eight games. Zero defeats. They did not win every game; they kept going together through the draws too. Being a great team takes more than one amazing afternoon. You prepare, help each other and try again.
Invite a quiet “wow” or a silent celebration.
Journal teacher note: Nobody beat Arsenal in the league that season. That’s why they were called the Invincibles.
sections.teacherNote: Nobody beat Arsenal in the league that season. That’s why they were called the Invincibles.

sections.label: Journal page 4  Greatness takes a team
blocks: Welcome to the trophy cabinet. Please admire the shiny objects with your eyes. My imaginary museum insurance is extremely imaginary.
Football clubs can win league competitions and cup competitions. A league rewards results across a season. Cups have rounds that teams try to progress through.
When one player scores, who else might have helped?
Accept passing, defending, saves, coaching, encouragement and other reasonable answers.
Exactly. The final touch gets the replay, but many people help make that moment possible. Think of a group project: the person holding the poster is not the only person who worked.
Journal teacher note: Which trophies do you think a football club can win? Let’s explore their history.
sections.teacherNote: Which trophies do you think a football club can win? Let’s explore their history.

sections.label: Journal page 5  Believe Prepare Improve
blocks: Believe. Prepare. Improve. Meet Arsène Wenger—our visionary, which means someone who can imagine what is possible and help people work toward it. He managed Arsenal for 22 years, led the Invincibles, and won three Premier League titles and seven FA Cups.

He could not just stand on the sideline and yell “Be amazing!” for 90 minutes. A manager has to prepare the team, choose a plan and help players develop. Wenger helped his team become great through preparation and teamwork.
You are the coach. A teammate misses a chance and says “I can’t do it.” What could you say, and what could you help them practise?
Take a helpful phrase and a practical next step. Open “You’re the coach. What is your next move?”

“Let’s try again. I can help you practise.” That is coaching we can use in football, math and during the mysterious disappearance of the glue-stick cap. Believing in someone means helping them take the next step.
Journal teacher note: Wenger helped his team become great through preparation and teamwork.
sections.teacherNote: Wenger helped his team become great through preparation and teamwork.

sections.label: Journal page 6  History makers
blocks: Arsenal Women are history makers. They won Europe’s top club competition in 2007 and again in 2025. The 2007 competition was called the UEFA Women’s Cup; by 2025 it was the Women’s Champions League. In the 2025 final, Arsenal beat Barcelona one–nil. Nil is football talk for zero.
Stina Blackstenius scored the winning goal. We will meet her in scouting. Keep that name in your scout notebook—which today may be your extremely powerful brain.
Does one winning goal explain everything about how a team won? Who else helped?
Take an answer about saves, defending, passing, preparation or encouragement.

Optional film: click the team photo, then Watch film in Cinema. This selects Only In The Land, the exact 1:49 Arsenal Women trailer. It opens the official player in another tab. Return to the Academy, then Return to journal → page 6. Skip playback to keep the short route.
That winning moment belongs to a whole team. People who start, people who come off the bench and people who help them prepare. Everyone’s work matters.
Journal teacher note: Their 2007 title was called the UEFA Women’s Cup. Their 2025 title was the Champions League!
sections.teacherNote: Their 2007 title was called the UEFA Women’s Cup. Their 2025 title was the Champions League!

sections.label: Journal page 7  Every player matters
blocks: Every player matters. Starting players, bench players, managers—everyone. You do not have to be the fastest runner or score the goal to help a team.
Touch Forward, Midfielder, Defender and Goalkeeper in turn.

Forwards find space and finish chances. Midfielders connect the team with passing and movement. Defenders protect the goal and build attacks. Goalkeepers make saves and can start the next attack. These are thinking jobs as well as moving jobs.

A substitute starts on the bench and may enter later. They watch, encourage and stay ready. A “super sub” is a nickname for a substitute who makes a big difference. Fewer minutes does not mean less importance.

Here is Mikel Merino. He is usually a midfielder. Against Leicester on 15 February 2025, he came on in the 69th minute and played up front. He scored in the 81st and 87th minutes. Two late goals, and Arsenal won two–nil. His team needed a different job, and he stepped in. That bench seat was not the end of his story.
Managers plan, encourage and help others improve. You can play, plan, encourage or help someone practise. You do not have to be on the pitch to belong or lead.
When you are waiting for your turn in class, how can you still help the team? Tell a partner.
Give 20 seconds; invite one answer. Listening, encouraging and staying ready all count.
Journal teacher note: You can play, plan, encourage or help others improve. You don’t have to be on the pitch to belong or lead.
sections.teacherNote: You can play, plan, encourage or help others improve. You don’t have to be on the pitch to belong or lead.

sections.label: Journal page 8  Watch the magic
blocks: We have reached the cinema. Imaginary popcorn is available at imaginary prices. Please do not eat the player cards.
Enter Cinema. Choose A Champion’s Story → Watch film for the 1:01 Merino trailer. Optional football action: Highlights → Merino: The Super Sub → Watch film. Choose one for the short route.

Lights down. Leaders rise. Keep an eye out for effort, preparation and support—and a player you like. Merino’s trailer is about working back from injury; his Leicester highlights show how staying ready can help a whole team.

Play the selected film, then return to the Academy. No review checkbox is required. The official player opens in another tab; access and ads depend on the device. If it will not play, use the no-video line below.
What did you notice? What could you say to a teammate having a hard day?
Now we are the supporters. We cheer for our team without putting anyone else down. Stadium energy, classroom volume. You can use your voice, a gentle clap or a hand motion.
Optional stadium moment: Stadium voices → North London Forever → Watch film. This is the 27-second official stadium clip you selected. Return to Cinema for our classroom cheer.
Call: ‘Arsenal!’ Class echoes: ‘Arsenal!’ Repeat three times with two gentle claps between calls. Finish with an open hand and silence.
Call: ‘Who belongs?’ Class: ‘Everyone!’ Call: ‘How do we lead?’ Class: ‘Help someone!’ Repeat once. These are our classroom words, not a recording of a stadium chant.
No-video line: ‘Merino’s story reminds us that recovering takes time, help and effort. Let’s be the teammates who encourage someone’s next step.’ Then do the cheers and continue.
Return to journal → page 8. Choose Next page for scouting, or take the optional Matchday stop on the next script card.
Journal teacher note: Now we watch some highlights. Keep an eye out for a player you like!
sections.teacherNote: Now we watch some highlights. Keep an eye out for a player you like!

sections.label: Optional Matchday challenge
blocks: On journal page 8, choose Explore this season.
Welcome to the sports desk. Let’s read the date first. This board is a snapshot, like a photograph of the league table. It does not change every second.
Read the displayed date, position, points and games played. Do not describe old figures as today’s standings. Use the official table link before class if updating the claim.
A win earns three points. A draw earns one. A loss earns zero. The board can change after matches, which is why our sports desk checks its dates. Even the sports desk has homework.
Scroll to Three questions. One team.
We have three questions and one team. Talk together before we choose. If we miss one, we get another chance. That is called learning, and we are unusually good at practising it.
Read each question and answer choices exactly as displayed. Let partners discuss; select the class answer. Use the feedback for a retry. Celebrate reaching 3 / 3 together.
Return to journal → page 8 → Next page → 9 / 12.

sections.label: Journal page 9  Your player Your story
sections.visual: Journal 9 / 12 · YOUR PLAYER YOUR STORY → Scouting
blocks: Welcome, scouts. Your mission is to find a player who interests you. You might notice a skill, a position, a country or a design. My scouting report currently says ‘enthusiastic and probably needs a snack.’ Let’s get more specific.
Explore the player cards. Choose William Saliba, then Kim Little, then Mikel Merino. Use the Men / Women filters if helpful; the All filter restores everyone.

Saliba is a defender from France, known here as the Calm Wall. Kim Little is a midfielder from Scotland, with experience and precise passing. Merino is a midfielder from Spain—the player we just met in the film.
Which quality would help our class today: calm, good communication, persistence, or something else? Tell us why.
If time allows, choose Stina Blackstenius and connect her profile with the 2025 final from journal page 6.
These digital profiles help us explore. Clicking a player does not reserve a physical card. The cards on our actual table are the choices available for the draft.
Give students 20 seconds to think of two or three possible choices. The same player can interest several people; everyone has different reasons.
Return to journal → page 9 → Next page → 10 / 12. Stay inside the Academy; player video-search links are not needed.
Journal teacher note: You might like their skills, position, country, or the design of the card.
sections.teacherNote: You might like their skills, position, country, or the design of the card.

sections.label: Journal page 10  Your turn is coming
sections.visual: Journal 10 / 12 · YOUR TURN IS COMING → Draft Day
blocks: It is Draft Day! Twenty-one students. Forty-two physical cards. Two cards each. Please remain seated until your classroom number is called. The excitement may stand up inside your brain.
The computer makes one random order of numbers 1 through 21. Your place in the order says nothing about your ability or importance. Everyone gets a turn.
Start the Draft → Shuffle the draft once. Then choose Reveal next pick.
With our first selection, Arsenal Academy welcomes… classroom number [read the large number]! Come choose your two cards.
Confirm the number, help the student choose two physical cards and mark your paper checklist. Let the student return before revealing the next number. Use a brief equal cheer for each student.
‘Our next scout is number [number]!’ ‘Number [number], your moment is here!’ ‘Welcome, number [number]—let’s find your team.’ Rotate these lines as you reveal each remaining pick.

Slow choice: ‘Pick the one that catches your eye. If you need help, tell me a color, country or role you like.’ Disappointment: ‘It is okay to feel disappointed. Let’s find another player or design you can enjoy.’
Volume reset: ‘Team check!’ Wait for ‘Ready!’ ‘We can be excited and still hear whose turn it is.’

Do not use Clear draft or reload during the draw; progress lives only in this open session. At 21 / 21, verify every student has two cards. If interrupted, use your paper record to finish the remaining turns.
Draft complete! Hold your cards carefully. Give the whole team one cheer, including the people who helped others choose.
Return to journal → page 10 → Next page → 11 / 12.
Journal teacher note: Everyone gets to choose a card. The order is random, and every player matters.
sections.teacherNote: Everyone gets to choose a card. The order is random, and every player matters.

sections.label: Journal page 11  How will you lead
blocks: How will you lead? We have our cards. Now we need something you cannot keep in a plastic sleeve: leadership. Great captains help others, stay calm and make their team better.

Tony Adams spent his whole senior playing career at Arsenal. He became captain at 21 and helped lead four league-title-winning teams. His story gives us loyalty and courage: keep showing up for your teammates, communicate and take responsibility when a job is difficult.
Someone is left out. What could a courageous teammate say?

Sol Campbell helped protect the goal in the Invincibles defense. A defender has to notice danger, communicate and keep making decisions under pressure. That gives us strength and composure. Composure means staying steady enough to think when things feel difficult.
Our group makes a mistake. What would staying calm and helping look like?
Accept taking a breath, listening and helping fix it together.

Wenger led that unbeaten team as manager. His job was to see what people could become and help them prepare. That gives us vision and belief: share a plan, help someone practise and notice their progress. A good leader does not need every answer; they can ask for help too.
Which will you try today: invite someone in, stay calm or help someone improve?

You do not need a badge to begin. A captain badge is a reminder to help, not a license to become the boss of everybody’s pencils. Next we will open the Vault and discover each captain’s leadership story.
Journal teacher note: Great captains help others, stay calm, and make their team better.
sections.teacherNote: Great captains help others, stay calm, and make their team better.

sections.label: Journal page 12  The Captains Vault
blocks: Our final stop is the Captain’s Vault. Six mystery shields hold six different stories about three legends. Two Tony Adams, two Sol Campbell and two Arsène Wenger. This is a surprise story draw; the six captains have already been chosen.
Open the Vault. Invite the first designated captain to choose one mystery shield, or point while you click.
Captain, choose your shield. Our dramatic drumroll is ten gentle fingertip taps… and stop. Let’s discover your story.
Read the revealed name, story title and short story exactly as shown. Then read its leadership lesson. Use the matching response below.
Tony Adams: ‘How could we stand by a teammate today?’ Sol Campbell: ‘How could we stay calm and help someone?’ Arsène Wenger: ‘What can we prepare or practise together?’
Let the captain offer one idea, choose a class suggestion or pass. Model ‘I can help someone join our group’ if needed. Participation does not require public speaking.
Next captain. Repeat until all six stories are revealed. After the sixth, choose Finish ceremony. Do not use Restart / reshuffle mid-ceremony.
Congratulations, captains—and congratulations to the whole academy. The badges are for six people; belonging is for all of us.
Before we finish, look at one of your cards and complete this thought: ‘Today I noticed…’ It could be a player, a skill or something kind someone did.
Take two responses. Finish with: ‘Who belongs?’ Class: ‘Everyone!’ ‘How do we lead?’ Class: ‘Help someone!’
Return to journal → page 12 → Back to clubhouse. Optional Newman Knights bonus: open Newman Knights and connect one displayed school value with something students did today.
Arsenal Academy session complete. Cards safe, teammates appreciated—and stadium announcer officially off duty.
Journal teacher note: We have a mystery draw for our six team captains!
sections.teacherNote: We have a mystery draw for our six team captains!
